contextBefore.narration: and we get deep inside Huck's moral wrestling with slavery in society. In Tom Sawyer, Tom remains somewhat opaque.
We are always watching him perform on a stage rather than truly living inside his head. That's fair criticism. The book is a performance, but what a performance
it is. Which brings us to the payoff. Let's bring it all back to that opening scene, the humid Saturday morning, the whitewashed fence.

beats.narration: We usually read that scene and laugh at the gullible boys like Ben Rogers who gave up their crisp apples and their kites to do Tom's grueling work.
We think they were fools who got conned. But maybe they weren't right. If we reframe the fence based on everything we've discussed today, maybe they weren't fools
at all. They were buying an experience. They were paying for the privilege of participating in something exclusive.
They wanted to feel special and Tom sold them that feeling. But Tom Sawyer was the one who understood the town best. He realized earlier than anyone else that work,
play, and heroism aren't inherent traits. They aren't laws of physics. They are just stories we agree to believe.
Value is a community agreement. And Tom was the master storyteller. He was. And as you go about your week, whether you're navigating corporate politics,
scrolling through branded content on social media, or just trying to get your kids to do their chores, consider Tom Sawyer not just as a barefoot boy in a 19th
century novel. Consider him as the ultimate prototype for the Gilded Age American businessman. Oh, absolutely.
He is the original marketer, creating demand out of thin air. He knew exactly how to package a product, even if that product was hard labor.
So look around your own life. Look at the structures you buy into.
